import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 779

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/779](https://www.erdosproblems.com/779)
-/

open Finset Nat

namespace Erdos779

/--
A Conjecture of Marian Deaconescu, see p.120 in https://doi.org/10.2307/2975810

[Needed to index shift in order to avoid trivial case $n = 0$,
where the conjecture is trivially false.]
-/
-- TODO(firsching): add formalization of the known cases for this conjecture:
-- n ≤ 1000, as well as the conjecture that p ≤ n^O(1)
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_779 (n : ℕ) (hn : n ≥ 1): let P := ∏ i ∈ range (n + 1), nth Nat.Prime i
    ∃ p, p.Prime ∧ (P + p).Prime ∧ nth Nat.Prime n < p ∧ p < P := by
  sorry

end Erdos779

reformulations.difference: The source assumes m > 1 and uses the first m primes, indexed from 1. Lean assumes n ≥ 1 and takes the product of Nat.nth Nat.Prime i for 0 ≤ i ≤ n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Set m = n + 1. Since Nat.nth Nat.Prime is zero-indexed, the Lean product is exactly the product of the source's first m primes, and Nat.nth Nat.Prime n is the source's p_m. The bijection n ↦ n + 1 takes n ≥ 1 to m > 1, with inverse m ↦ m - 1. Both primality requirements and both strict bounds on the existential witness are unchanged. This equivalence was proved as Review779.source_equivalence in /workspace/review/scratch.lean, without using the conjecture or any sorry axiom.

sources_consulted: https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/Erdos.html — searched the bibliography for the cited article

Čejchan, Křížek, and Somer, On Remarkable Properties of Primes Near Factorials and Primorials, Journal of Integer Sequences 25 (2022), §3 and Remark 5: https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL25/Krizek/krizek3.tex
Meštrović, arXiv:1202.3670, §1.3 (primorial background), LaTeX source: https://arxiv.org/e-print/1202.3670
review.notes: The sole declaration faithfully states the conjecture in the archived source. Nat.nth's default-zero case is unreachable for the infinite prime predicate. Lean checks verified witnesses for n = 1, 2, 3, 4 and refuted the excluded n = 0 case; the smallest allowed case is P = 6, p = 5, P + p = 11. The July 2026 source snapshot and the currently retrieved problem database both record the problem as falsifiable/open, consistent with the category. The finite verification and polynomial-bound remarks are only TODOs, not additional declarations. Live erdosproblems.com and JSTOR requests returned browser challenges; the full 1983 article was unavailable, but the archived problem page and all four archived forum comments were readable and unambiguous.
